articles.title_zh: Putin observes military drills in the Urals involving troops from China and other nations
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, center left, visits the Center-2026 military exercises at the Chebarkulsky training ground outside Chebarkul, Chelyabinsk region, Russia, Friday. (Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)
MOSCOW — Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday attended military drills in the Ural Mountains involving troops from China and several other countries.
Putin visited a firing range in the Chelyabinsk region to observe the final stage of the Center-2026 maneuvers. The exercises were combined with the Interaction-2026 drills held by members of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, a Moscow-dominated security alliance of several former Soviet nations.
Putin said Center-2026 involved 47,000 troops training to repel an attack at 11 firing ranges and in the Caspian Sea. The drills began Monday and will run through Saturday.
About 6,000 troops from Russia and other countries took part in the final phase at Chebarkulsky, Putin said. Delegations from 55 nations attended as observers, he added.
The drills included military contingents from Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, as well as troops from China, Mongolia and Pakistan, according to Russian news reports.
During his visit, Putin inspected an array of weapons, including new jet-powered Geran drones used by the Russian military against Ukraine.
Putin’s inspection came a day after Russia warned NATO that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military bloc try to cut off its western exclave from the rest of the country.

articles.content_orig:
Kazakhstan is at the centre of US efforts to build a new supply chain for the metal, but analysts say China’s lead will be difficult to overcome
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.
The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.
According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of manufacturing drill bits had risen by as much as 50 per cent over the past year. The company is responding by shifting production towards steel-bodied models, even as bits containing more tungsten typically last longer when cutting through hard, abrasive rock.

articles.title_orig: G-7 agrees to release oil reserves to reduce fuel prices after U.S. pressure
articles.title_zh: G-7 agrees to release oil reserves to reduce fuel prices after U.S. pressure
articles.content_orig:
Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves
The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.
President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Watch: Why did Trump threaten to ban US diesel exports?
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped Â£2 a litre for the first time on Friday .
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
Why UK diesel prices have breached the Â£2 per litre mark
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title_orig: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.title_zh: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.content_orig:
DM Vans builds its camper vans today in a state-of-the-art, 20,000-square-foot facility in Rifle.
The company has come a long way from the original production site: the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
DM Vans co-founder Matt Fesler built this first van out of necessity.
“I wanted something I could travel through the mountains with, bring my skis, bring my bikes, bring my golf clubs, and stay in comfortably,” Fesler said. “At the time, there really wasn’t something out there on the market that fit what I was looking for within my budget.”
Felser was a teacher at Vail Mountain School at the time and needed a vehicle that could serve as a portable base camp for his adventures.
With the help of YouTube tutorials and some friends, the first Dave and Matt, or DM, van came to fruition in the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
Fesler and his friend, and eventual DM Vans co-founder, Dave Ramsay, soon realized that they had done more than build the vehicle that Fesler was looking for.
The pair “realized that (they) had something, something that was simple, reliable, easier to use than what was on the market, and obviously more affordable,” Fesler said.
After living in that first van for nine months, which he “loved to death,” Fesler got the itch to build more.
“So I sold that first one, used that to build two, sold two, built four, sold four, built eight, and yeah, here we are, eight years later, and 800 vans,” Fesler said.
The 800 Ram ProMaster vans which DM vans transformed into parking-spot-sized homes are now spread across 48 states, and the company shows no signs of slowing down.
Although the 30-person team, and sheer scale of the operation are a far cry from the early days of DM Vans, some things have stayed the same.
“We’ve used the tagline ‘everything you need, nothing you don’t’ from day one,” Fesler said. “That was kind of how I wanted to approach it in terms of something that was simple and reliable that would get me from A to B comfortably and allow me to stay there and pursue my passions, and it is amazing how that design philosophy has stayed from day one through now.”
That does not mean DM Vans has shied away from technological advances to improve their product, however.
With smaller, lighter and more powerful lithium batteries on the market, DM Vans can run heating, air conditioning, running water, refrigeration and other appliances off relatively small power supply.
Using a computer numerical control, or CNC, machine, the company can cut out wooden parts with precision and ease.
DM Vans hopes to build 145 vans in the coming year.
The combination of the “van-life” boom and navigating the coronavirus pandemic gave the pair their fair share of obstacles to navigate.
“Dave (Ramsay) and I joke a lot that we very much had the best MBA program you could possibly go on in our eight-year journey here of the highest of highs, lowest of lows, but are really excited for the stability that we now have as a business, the incredible employees we have in Rifle and around Colorado,” Fesler said.
After eight years of successful business and growth, Fesler is proud of how far the company has come.
“The numbers of businesses that go out of business after five years are staggering, right? To make it to 10 is truly something that would be that peak moment for us, and so just being here doing something that we love is the thing that makes me the most proud,” Fesler said.

articles.title_orig: What to know about Christa Pike, her failed execution and what happens next
articles.title_zh: What to know about Christa Pike, her failed execution and what happens next
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, 50, remains in a hospital early Thursday after a botched execution in Tennessee.
Pike, the lone woman on death row, was set to be the first female in more than 200 years the state had put to death, according to historical records .
However, after she was injected twice with a lethal drug, Pike did not die, and she was transferred to an “off-site medical facility,” a spokesperson for the Department of Correction told NBC News. Attorneys for Pike said late Wednesday that she was being treated at a hospital but that they did not know her condition.
Here’s what to know about her case.
In 1995, Knoxville police said Pike and two teenage accomplices had worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19.
Police said Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike does not dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They had asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, was likely to create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state has not denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court appeared to be Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.” The high court denied her petition Tuesday evening.
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken” that the governor would not be granting clemency.
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
Before she learned Monday that Lee would not intervene in her case, Pike wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser, that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of the time when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also pointed to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time.
Tadaryl Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and was sentenced to probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police that she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous, believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention.
Pike’s lawyers said her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers said her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed in solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Pike’s lawyers asked Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider whether any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse.
Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. Pike’s case, she added, is a lesson in the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.
May Martinez, the mother of victim Slemmer, is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.
Martinez recalled that, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts were not buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. She had to pick up Slemmer’s skull from the courthouse, and she remembers that the medical examiner’s office mailed her other parts later. (The office said it rarely retains human remains as it did 30 years ago because of better technology, enhanced photography and lab work.)
“We had her buried in a Catholic cemetery,” Martinez said. “And she had to be dug up every time they mailed me body parts.”
Recently, she said, she has refused to communicate with Pike directly. The only way she can get justice now is when she watches Pike be executed.
“I will sit there with her picture in my hand,” Martinez said of her daughter, “and as she gets hooked up to a needle to go to sleep, she can look at the picture.”
Given the rarity of the execution of a female prisoner, Tennessee corrections officials said they would make an effort to fulfill certain requests made by Pike. They included using female guards when she was moved from her all-women’s prison in Nashville to the nearby Riverbend Maximum Security Institution within 24 hours of her planned execution. An all-female execution team may also have been assigned.

articles.title_orig: Lemon Hill hosted the world for Fan Fest. Now, Philadelphia will spend millions to improve it for locals.
articles.title_zh: Lemon Hill hosted the world for Fan Fest. Now, Philadelphia will spend millions to improve it for locals.
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA Fan Festival brought hundreds of thousands of people from across the planet to Philadelphia's Lemon Hill for a celebration of soccer this summer. Now, as the massive stage and vendor tents have left the natural scenery, the park will undergo a different transformation.
"In spite of the fact that Fan Fest did take away the park for a while, I think it became sort of the momentum generator for what's to come," Aparna Palantino, who heads the city's Capital Program Office, said.
CBS News Philadelphia was the only TV station to get a first look at the nearly $7 million in upgrades and enhancements planned for the rolling hills in East Fairmount Park.
At the center of the project is a new 43,500-square-foot age-inclusive playground to replace the current structure, which has been in place for decades.
Palantino said the playground will incorporate the park's natural features, like slides that use Lemon Hill's natural hillside.
"We wanted it to fit within the context of the park. It is a lovely, very natural, pristine setting. Has a lot of historical character. And it was important for us to maintain that," Palantino said.
Aside from the playground, the plan includes renovations to the popular basketball courts at Lemon Hill and to the nearby baseball field. Two new ADA-accessible picnic pavilions with seating will be built. More than 50 light posts are set to be added around the park, increasing lighting and safety. And crews plan to plant more than 100 new trees.
"Across the site, we want to return a lot of the tree canopy that was lost over the years," Palantino said.
Officials said the city has looked into making many of these changes for years but never had the funding to do it. That changed with the FIFA Fan Festival, when officials built partnerships that got the project across the finish line.
Officials said Philadelphia Soccer 2026 and the William Penn Foundation will kick in a total of $4 million for the plans, with the city picking up the rest of the bill.
Some enhancements were also made prior to Fan Fest opening in June. New walking paths were added for better access to the park. Roads were paved. Trees were trimmed, and invasive plants were cleared out.
But for this portion, Palantino said they focused on what community members told them they wanted here.
"We had over 200 individual community members participate in over 300 surveys to get their feedback on what they wanted to see," Palantino said. "We have very good stewards and neighbors who take care of this park on a regular basis. And it was really important that all of their voices were heard."
Signs are already posted showing some of the planned changes. The current playground and basketball courts are fenced off, getting ready for the changes. City officials on Monday will host a ceremonial planting of the first new tree.
Officials hope the work can be done and upgrades open to the public in the spring.

articles.title_orig: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
articles.title_zh: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
articles.content_orig:
Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.
Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
“The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame.
Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Now, Apple is setting the record straight. In explaining why it was going to make changes to the FDA permission setting, the company wrote:
Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.
As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.
Apple didn’t name Meta, Muse, or any other app or developer by name. Even though there are no known reports of other apps abusing FDA to read messages and browsing history, it’s certainly possible Friday’s statement wasn’t referring to the Muse incident. Then again, the timing of the announcement—coming on the heels of a major social media uproar—makes the possibility likely. And at a minimum, Apple’s statements seem to contradict Singleton’s denial that it’s not possible for Muse to read Messages content without the connector enabled. Meta PR didn’t respond to questions sent Friday.
Apple’s announcement came 11 days after Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that allowed any app or code running on a Mac—including commands injected through the increasingly effective ClickFix attacks—to take full control of the AI assistant . From there, the attacker could access the same resources Muse could. It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse from its platform because, Amazon said, all such apps “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”
Taken together, the events suggest that Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it must have to work as billed by Meta. People who use the assistant should configure permissions carefully, though as Aten’s experience suggests, that precaution only goes so far.

articles.title_orig: Madari: India's street magicians fighting to keep a disappearing art alive
articles.title_zh: Madari: India's street magicians fighting to keep a disappearing art alive
articles.content_orig:
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says.  "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention,  and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

Dominic Rosales, a 16-year-old goaltender from Hollister, has been selected to represent Team USA's junior inline hockey team at the 2026 World Skate Games in Asunción, Paraguay, marking the biggest tournament of his career.
"I just want to, like, take the most out of it, experience how South America is going to be, having to represent Team USA. Play with my friends, you know, I think that will be the most I want to take out of it. Obviously, winning a gold medal would be cool too," Rosales said.
A gold medal would be a fitting achievement for Rosales, who has already proven himself as one of the nation's elite young goaltenders.
Rosales grew up watching his father, Diego, play as a goalie, inspiring him to pursue the position himself. His passion for the sport started early, even leading him to dress up as a goalie for Halloween.
"Me and my buddy just MacGyvered that thing. We just got a bunch of tape, cardboard, and hard foam, and we made his own little set. He was super happy. After Halloween, he used it every single day outside. He was able to slide across in the living room, and he thought he was the next goalie, you know? And it worked," Diego said.
Diego has been instrumental in supporting his son's dream, working three jobs over the years to ensure Dominic could pursue his passion for hockey.
"I think the most rewarding things out of this, sure, I'll take another job, another shift, do extra jobs here and there. I think the fact that he loves the sport makes it so much worth it, right? And we can look past all the rest of it," Diego said.
As Rosales prepares to compete on the world stage, he carries the pride of his hometown with him.
"It fills me with pride because I know Hollister will have my back and support me. They've been supporting me with this journey. I think, definitely coming back, I'll have a lot of pride. I'm happy I'm able to represent Hollister, a small town," Rosales said.

In a text message sent to customers today, AT&T acknowledged that some iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on its network are experiencing cellular issues .
AT&T said that customers should immediately update to iOS 27.0.1 , despite the fact that many affected users have said that the update does not resolve the issues. There are now at least thousands of users that have experienced this problem, according to discussion topics across the Apple Support Community , Reddit , and MacRumors Forums .
Here is what the text message says:
Hi, it's AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.
Apple's release notes for iOS 27.0.1 did not mention a fix for AT&T cellular issues. Rather, the update fixed a Face ID issue on the iPhone 18 Pro models.
As we reported last week, affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users are unable to connect to the AT&T network for phone calls, text messages, or data either persistently or intermittently, and their devices typically enter SOS mode as a result. The underlying cause has not been confirmed, and Apple has yet to publicly comment on the matter.
Notably, the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only new iPhone unveiled last month that is equipped with a Qualcomm cellular modem . The smaller iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo are equipped with Apple's C2 modem worldwide, as is the iPhone 18 Pro Max in all other countries. However, it is unclear if this is a contributing factor.
If a software issue is identified, then another update such as iOS 27.0.2 may be required. If there is a hardware issue, though, then this would obviously be a much bigger problem. We will provide further updates as new information becomes available.
(P.S. There is some irony in AT&T sending a text message to warn iPhone 18 Pro Max users that they might not be able to send or receive text messages.)

articles.title_orig: A 20-year-old Amish woman with leukemia got measles and died in Pa.’s largest outbreak in three decades
articles.title_zh: A 20-year-old Amish woman with leukemia got measles and died in Pa.’s largest outbreak in three decades
articles.content_orig:
After measles swept through her household, the young woman wanted to get vaccinated. Her doctor said she couldn't because she had leukemia and the treatments had weakened her immune system.
The headstone had not yet been placed Thursday on the freshly dug grave where a 20-year-old Amish woman was buried this week amid the rolling clover fields and dairy farms at the edge of suburban Philadelphia.
Newly wed, and receiving treatment for blood cancer, she was the last of nine siblings sickened when measles swept through her unvaccinated family’s home on a one-lane road in Lancaster County.
At first, the home remedies that eased their symptoms seemed to help her, too: Soothing the fever with bath soaks. Calming the rash with coconut or olive oil. Cloistering in a dark room to ease light sensitivity.
Then her fever spiked. She struggled to breathe and had to sleep sitting up in a recliner in the living room, her maternal grandmother recalled.
Her family does not operate cars, in keeping with Amish beliefs, so they hired a driver to take her to the emergency department at Hershey Medical Center about an hour away. She died about two weeks later in the intensive care unit there, her grandmother said.
Speaking on the porch of her stone farmhouse, the grandmother described the family’s experience with Pennsylvania’s largest measles outbreak in three decades, now the nation’s largest. At her request, The Inquirer withheld her name and that of her deceased granddaughter to protect the family’s privacy.
She said her granddaughter ultimately developed double pneumonia and died after the family decided to discontinue use of a ventilator.
The cancer made her especially vulnerable to a virus as contagious as measles, which will infect 9 in 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed.
“Her immune system wasn’t built up,” the grandmother said. “She just couldn’t take it with the measles.”
Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday its fifth measles-related death , revealing only that the latest fatality was an unvaccinated Lancaster County resident. Health officials did not provide further details, citing privacy laws.
But it appears from the grandmother’s account, along with other records and news reports, that three of the five deaths occurred in adults with measles. Other reported deaths included an 18-year-old Amish woman from Mifflin County and a 40-year-old from Jefferson County with severe respiratory conditions. Two Amish infants in Lancaster County who had confirmed measles cases also died. All five cases involved people who were unvaccinated, either by choice or because they were too young to receive vaccines.
The number of deaths in adults is striking, said Paul Offit, who heads the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. Widespread childhood vaccinations had eradicated the disease in the United States, leaving mostly children too young to be vaccinated at high risk in recent decades. Now multiple generations of unvaccinated children are adults, exposing wider vulnerabilities across the state, Offit said.
“We’re aging out a population that was never vaccinated,” he said.
After learning the details of the 20-year-old’s death from The Inquirer, Offit explained that measles commonly leads to pneumonia.
“The measles virus reproduces itself in the lungs and can cause severe and occasionally fatal infection,” he said.
The young woman, the second oldest in a line of nine siblings, ages 6 to 22, feared getting measles in the outbreak in Lancaster County, her grandmother said.
About two years ago, she was diagnosed with leukemia, a blood cancer, and began medical treatment with the help of an “English” neighbor — as Amish call outsiders — to drive her to her medical appointments.
The treatment regimen of chemo and steroids further weakened her immune system. She knew she was at risk of more severe sickness from a viral infection like measles, which started spreading throughout her family in the late summer.
Her eight siblings, her parents, and her new husband all got sick, the grandmother said.
Along with home remedies, family members drank extra fluids to stay hydrated, the grandmother said.
“They weren’t worried,” the grandmother said. “ Measles just has to take its course.”
Although no one in the household was vaccinated, they are not opposed to the vaccine based on Amish beliefs. They believe it’s an individual choice, she said, and many Amish people opt not to get vaccinated because they “don’t know what’s in it.”
“We wouldn’t tell people not to get vaccinated,” the grandmother said. “It’s up to each person.”
As illness spread in her household, her granddaughter grew more worried about getting the virus than about the vaccine that medical authorities have long considered safe and effective.
She asked her doctor if she could get a measles vaccination. Her doctor said no. “She wasn’t allowed to get the shot because she was on chemo,” the grandmother said.
The measles vaccine contains a live but weakened virus, and her granddaughter was already immunocompromised from the leukemia treatment.
After getting measles, her granddaughter began to feel better in early September. She picked vegetables from the family’s garden to make soup using tomato juice as the broth. She canned jars for the coming cold months, her grandmother said.
“She had good days,” the grandmother said.

Then, in mid-September, she spiked a high fever, and her breathing became labored.
“She could hardly breath. Her lungs were just in bad shape,” she said.
The Amish typically only seek emergency hospital treatment until “sometimes we’re dying,” the grandmother said, recalling how her husband got chided by a doctor in 2018 for waiting too long to get the heart surgery he desperately needed.
“We do what we can at home,” she said. “We have so many natural things we can do.”
By Sept. 11, the family knew it was time to take her granddaughter for emergency care at Hershey Medical Center.
At Hershey’s ER, doctors gave her a chest X-Ray, but sent her home before reading it, the grandmother said.
“They wouldn’t do anything for her. They didn’t want her there,” she said. (A Hershey spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment on Friday.)
A Hershey provider later called and left a voicemail message asking the family to bring her back. Although the family has a phone in their house, the grandmother said they rarely use it. With the ringer off, all calls go to voicemail, she said.
A driver took them back to the hospital, where she was admitted on Sept. 14. An ultrasound showed fluid between the lining of her lungs and in her lungs. She was diagnosed with double pneumonia, her grandmother said.
Hospital staff hooked her up to supplemental oxygen.
“They had the oxygen up as far as they could and she still had to work to breathe,” the grandmother said.
About a week later, they moved her to the intensive care unit, where they sedated her so they could put her on a ventilator while intubated.
The hospital allowed two family members at a time to sit by her bed. Her granddaughter’s young husband and the girl’s mother sat vigil, the grandmother said.
As she continued to deteriorate, life support was the only remaining option, and it carried the risk of neurological complications, including brain death.
The family didn’t want that, the grandmother said. “They couldn’t do anything more,” she said.
They turned off the oxygen and shut off the ventilator, Family members, including her new husband’s parents, gathered around her bed.
She died with a breathing tube still in her mouth, the grandmother said.
More than 300 people came to the family’s home on Monday for the funeral service and viewing. She was buried in a cemetery near the family’s home, about a month before what would have been her first wedding anniversary.

articles.title_orig: As Trump's proposed arch looms over D.C., protesters pin their hopes on the midterms
articles.title_zh: As Trump's proposed arch looms over D.C., protesters pin their hopes on the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators gathered Thursday morning to protest Trump's proposed arch, which would stand in a traffic circle on the bridge connecting the National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery. Saul Loeb/AFP hide caption
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Dozens of activists gathered at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., at rush hour Thursday to protest the 250-foot-tall arch that President Trump wants to build there.
Veterans, retirees and lawmakers spoke out — against its scale, its cost, its lack of Congressional approval, its gaudiness, its intrusion on nearby Arlington National Cemetery and more — next to a mockup made of tarp. The real arch, they said, would be 32 times taller.
"It's the wrong monument, in the wrong place, at the wrong time, dedicated to the wrong man," said Jon Gundersen, a retired Army veteran and former Foreign Service officer who is one of the Vietnam War veterans suing the Trump administration over the arch.
Gundersen traveled from South Carolina to speak at Thursday's protest, which was billed as "Vets over Vanity. It was organized in part by Public Citizen, the group leading that lawsuit. He told NPR that it was "heartening" to see so much support for their cause.
"Anyone I talk to, whether Republican or Democrat, they say it's a waste of money and it's not how you honor vets," he said.
Many speakers were especially concerned about the impact of an arch towering over nearby Arlington National Cemetery, and criticized the lack of input from veterans and gold star families in the process.
"I am pissed that the five-time draft dodging coward of a commander-in-chief sitting over there in the White House dares to dishonor the men and women of this country who have put on her collars and sacrificed and served and now lay at rest in the hallowed grounds of Arlington National Cemetery," said Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., who said she and her husband will join them one day.
The White House has told NPR that the arch will "enhance the visitor experience" at the cemetery and serve "as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes." But Duckworth and others say a better way to honor veterans would be to spend money on improving services for them, not on a triumphal arch with an observation deck.
Protesters stand Thursday in Memorial Circle near a mockup of Trump's arch, which they say would be 32 times taller. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
"Imagine tourists coming up to this arch looking at the 24 to 27 funerals up there in Arlington," Gundersen said. "It's not only wrong and inappropriate, it's obscene and should never [be] done."
During the half-hour of rapid-fire speeches, the crowd burst into loud applause, sporadic chants of "no arch!" and, at one point, a coordinated rendition of We Shall Overcome . Cyclists and commuters passing by offered supportive waves and honks.
Planes flew overhead every few minutes, a constant reminder that the arch would stand along the approach of one of the nation's busiest airport runways. Several of the speakers addressed the aviation safety concerns raised by the arch and by Trump's recent announcement that the structure will house military drones and snipers .
"Who are the snipers going to shoot — the families at the graves or the tourists at the Lincoln Memorial?" Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said from the podium. "The real explanation is Trump thinks he's going to lose in court, and maybe if he shouts national security, the Supreme Court will care."
The White House, Department of Interior and Federal Aviation Administration have not responded to NPR's questions about the military complex. The Trump administration has not elaborated publicly on what rebranding the structure could mean for the ongoing federal approval process, despite mounting confusion.
But it did drop hints in a meeting earlier this week.
Administration officials told historic preservation groups in a Tuesday Zoom call that they were unaware of any new submissions and planned to move forward with the original arch proposal, according to a transcript and recording later shared with NPR.
And — despite the public pushback, an ongoing lawsuit and many unanswered questions — that proposal is hurtling towards final federal approval.
The arch is widely expected to come before the National Capital Planning Commission at its next meeting in early November.
As part of the required federal review process, the National Park Service had been in conversation with outside groups to negotiate how to build the arch while doing the least harm to the dozens of nearby protected landmarks . The park service had already dismissed experts' suggestions to build the arch elsewhere.
Then, the last week of September — just days after Trump's military complex announcement — the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation terminated the review process altogether. That was announced in an email to historic preservation groups, reviewed by NPR.
Charles Birnbaum, who participated in the process as the head of The Cultural Landscape Foundation, said he was appalled that the council cut the review short after only two meetings. He recalled this happening only twice in the 15 years he previously spent working for the National Park Service.
"Projects go to the advisory council when there is a stalemate that people have tried to negotiate with state preservation officers, with stakeholders, and there is an authenticity to that process," Birnbaum said.
Instead, the advisory council now says it will give its recommendations directly to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum by Oct. 7.
"They're going to force this upon the process and they're going to nullify outside voices. And what this is symbolic of is where the administration is taking the nation," said Birnbaum, referring to the same council's efforts to roll back protections for historic sites nationwide . Separately, a bipartisan permitting reform bill gaining traction in Congress would also weaken those protections.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., speaks to demonstrators at Thursday's event. His efforts to block federal funding for the arch were rejected by a GOP senator earlier in the week. Allison Robbert/AP hide caption
Protesters on Thursday vowed not to let the arch proceed — but braced for the possibility that it might.
"We have to continue to call in to our senators, our congresspeople, and let them say no to this arc," said Julius D. "JD" Spain Sr., a member of the Arlington County Board. "And if it is built, if somehow it is built, I will get my chisel and I'll be right over there with everybody tearing it down."
That prompted some of the loudest applause of the morning. Beyer, whose district includes Arlington, told NPR afterward that there is a "huge body of people ready to protest the moment they see a shovel."
"I don't know how this will play out, whether we end up with tents or hunger strikes, but I know that the American people are ready to protest in any way they can," he said.
There is another possibility, at least in theory: Congress could stop the arch by blocking federal funding from going towards the project. Earlier this week, a single Republican senator blocked Democrats' attempts to stop the construction of the arch as well as the demolition of the Kennedy Center.
"We could stop this today if the Republican majority stepped up and grew a backbone and would oppose Trump," Duckworth told NPR in a phone interview Wednesday.
Next month's midterm elections could change the balance of power in Congress — and, if Democrats prevail, spell bad news for the arch starting in January.

articles.title_orig: UK charges 2 Iranian men over alleged Yom Kippur terror plot in Manchester
articles.title_zh: UK charges 2 Iranian men over alleged Yom Kippur terror plot in Manchester
articles.content_orig:
Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to attack the Jewish community in Manchester on the eve of Yom Kippur, the latest in a wave of antisemitic attacks in the UK this year.
London’s Metropolitan police named the suspects as 36-year-old Salam Ahmadyan of Liverpool and 34-year-old Rahman Salehi of Salford, who were arrested on September 20, on the eve of the holiest day in Judaism, a year after a deadly synagogue attack in Manchester. They were charged on Friday with “engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts,” police said.
Authorities also said the two men are allegedly in contact with a third person who may be in Iran in relation to the alleged plot.
“These are extremely serious charges and allegations and have come about from a joint CTP (Counter Terror Policing) investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services,” said Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for CTP.
Evans said the investigation helped disrupt what is believed to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community, but that authorities do not believe there to be an ongoing threat to the public related to the attempted attack.
The charges come a year after a deadly car ramming and stabbing attack outside a Manchester synagogue killed at least two people. They also come just a day after another Iranian national with dual British citizenship was arrested on suspicion of terror offenses linked to an alleged plot to target a UK airbase used by the US military in Fairford, western England.
The 25-year-old was arrested in Westminster, London, after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident – something the Iranian government has denied.
Authorities have said the airbase incident is not believed to be connected with the latest attempted attack on Manchester’s Jewish community.
“This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran,” Evans said. “While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”
The UK has seen a wave of antisemitic attacks this year, including assaults on synagogues and other communal buildings. The British government subsequently announced extra police forces to protect Jewish areas across the country.
“We know how concerning this news will be to Jewish communities in Greater Manchester, and beyond,” Greater Manchester Police Deputy Chief Constable Terry Woods said. “We know this is particularly acute on the calendar anniversary of last year’s terrorist atrocity at the Heaton Park synagogue, and during the Jewish High Holy Days.”
Woods said the “ongoing and robust” policing plans across Jewish communities would remain in place as authorities work closely with community leaders and British Counter-Terrorism Police.

articles.title_orig: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.title_zh: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.content_orig:
A nonprofit environmental group working with primates in Sebangau National Park says the dry peatlands can be a catalyst to more destruction.
(CN) â Since early August, wildfires have devastated the fragile rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, causing widespread toxic air across Indonesia. Itâs affected most communities in all parts of the region of Kalimantan, a part of the worldâs third largest island under Indonesiaâs governance.
The fires are fueled by shifting El NiÃ±o climate patterns, causing severe drought and extremely dry conditions in the islandâs peatlands, among the planetâs most effective carbon-capturing ecosystems and vital habitat for wildlife found nowhere else in the world.
Sebangau National Park in Central Kalimantan is home to an estimated 6,000 to 9,000 critically endangered Bornean orangutans, one of the islandâs largest populations. The nonprofit Borneo Nature Foundation said a fire crossed the park boundary for the first time in early September.
âOur teams pushed it back, and it was largely confined to sedge and open peat, but some reforestation sites are impacted,â Dr. Susan Cheyne, the Science Director for the Borneo Nature Foundation and the Vice Chair for the International Union for the Conservation of Nature special project group for small apes, said in an email to Courthouse News.
âOur priority is to keep fire out of the forest, because that protects every orangutan in it at once,â she said. Cheyne and her colleagues monitor and document conditions in Borneo, while volunteer firefighting crews work to keep fires out of orangutan habitat and nearby villages. Capturing and removing the apes is âa last resort,â Cheyne said.
Sebangau is also home to several of the worldâs rarest primates, including the largest known population of Bornean white-bearded gibbons, an ape Cheyne has studied for over 20 years.
Gibbons are known for their musical vocalizations, or âsongs.â Males sing alone in the morning before females join them in duets later in the day.
âDuring the 2006 fires I found that gibbons sang less often and sang shorter songs on smoky days. Their song is how they defend territory and keep pair bonds, so this matters,â said Cheyne. âA similar pattern has since been recorded in wild Bornean orangutans exposed to wildfire smoke.â
Gibbons rarely come to the ground, and fire survivors are often left in small, isolated forest patches with little food. Other primates, including red langurs and long-tailed and southern pig-tailed macaques, are found only in Southeast Asia, and each fire further reduces their numbers. Little is known about how fires affect nocturnal slow lorises and western tarsiers, Cheyne said.
The national park includes vast peat swamps, made of partly decomposed plant material accumulated over thousands of years. In parts of Sebangau, the peat dome reaches 12 meters deep.
Peatlands are naturally waterlogged, like giant sponges that do not burn. But in the 1990s and early 2000s, illegal loggers dug hundreds of canals to float timber out of the forest. Those canals continue draining the peat, causing it to dry out and become fuel.
âIn a long dry season like this one, a dried-out peat swamp is a tinderbox,â said Cheyne.
âWhat makes peat fires so hard to fight is that they burn downwards and sideways, not just across the surface. Fire smolders underground through the dry peat, sometimes for weeks, long after the flames above have gone out. These are sometimes called zombie fires.â
Peat fires are particularly dangerous because from the surface, a person may see nothing amiss, perhaps âjust a thin wisp of smoke,â Cheyne said, while a meter below the peat burns and can set nearby tree roots aflame, easily toppling them. And peat fires also produce dense, toxic smoke.
Cheyne said since 2015, the foundation and local crews have built over 1,000 dams to block drainage canals, planted almost a million trees, drilled hundreds of water boreholes, and increased support for up to eight fire teams.
âThat preparation is why we are holding,â she said. But itâs still a tenuous situation. For the short-term, Cheyne said, the goal is to keep the firefighting teams in the field fed, equipped and safe, which costs about $100 a day per team. It also means investing in equipment, such as thermal drones that can detect underground peat fires and rewetting the peat, so it doesnât reignite. The foundation, she said, is actively seeking donations from international bodies, advocacy groups and concerned individuals.
While hotspots in Kalimantan have declined since the beginning of the month, according to the foundation, rains are not expected until late October or November.
âWe are not out of this yet,â said Cheyne.
Cheyne said Borneo Nature Foundation Internationalâs co-founder Simon Husson recently passed a troop of monkeys on a river trip and they moved through trees beside mile after mile of burned riverbank.
âThat is the picture,â she said. âLife hanging on right at the edge.â

articles.title_orig: FAA Says 737 MAX Software Glitch Doesn’t Pose Safety Issue
articles.title_zh: FAA Says 737 MAX Software Glitch Doesn’t Pose Safety Issue
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it has determined a new software glitch on some Boeing 737 Max aircraft isn't a flight-safety issue.
The determination paves the way to certification for the last model in the company's best-selling family of airplanes, the 737 Max 10, just as Boeing seeking to sell and deliver more aircraft after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing flagged the software issue, which could affect certain landing procedures, last month and the FAA on Monday said it was reviewing to determine if it poses a safety of flight issue.
"Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern," the FAA said. "The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
The FAA said on Friday that it will issue a special bulletin to airlines on how to recognize and respond to the issue if it arises.
The agency convened a review board on Friday to assess the issue. Participants included FAA experts on airframes, flight controls, propulsion, flight testing and others.
"As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue," the agency said.
U.S. airlines said they're not affected by the issue since they could revert to older versions of the software, but the problem raised questions about certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10, which Boeing and airlines expected to come in early fall.
The Max 10 is the largest in the family of airplanes and would be the last of the Max lineup to win government certification to fly. The FAA approved the Max 7 , the smallest in the Max family, in August.
Chief executives of 737 Max 10 customers, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, earlier this week brushed off concerns about the aircraft's certification delays.

articles.title_orig: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.title_zh: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.content_orig:
High school students face no shortage of challenges, from maintaining top grades to balancing extracurricular activities. But for Wayzata High School sophomore Aakya Manamperi, her pursuits extend far beyond the classroom. In fact, they stretch all the way across the globe.
Manamperi, 15, is a second-degree black belt and one of the nation’s top-ranked karate competitors in her age group.
Later this fall, she will travel to Spain to compete on the global stage at the World Karate Commission (WKC) World Championships.
Inside Dojo Karate in Medina, Manamperi serves as a patient instructor, guiding young students through fundamental martial arts skills. But don’t let her calm demeanor fool you. When she steps onto the tournament floor, she’s a force to be reckoned with.
“It’s kind of a really male-dominated sport,” Manamperi said. “So, being a female, and a female of color, it’s really important for me to go out there and represent.”
Aakya Manamperi teaches karate to a group of kids at Dojo Karate in Medina.
Manamperi began practicing karate at age 6. Achieving elite national status has required years of rigorous discipline and daily training.
“I’ve been training two hours every single day,” Manamperi said. “The first hour is mostly cardio, training drills, working on technique. And the second hour is just focusing on my kata that I’m going to be competing.”
Kata, her primary discipline, consists of detailed, high-intensity sequences of movements. Judges evaluate performance based on technique, power, rhythm, balance and presentation—an evaluation process that has earned Manamperi an impressive collection of trophies and medals over the years.
Her dedication has drawn praise from local mentors, including Dojo Karate Medina owner Javier Franco, who noted the positive influence she has on younger students.
“Of course, this is a big impact on the students,” Franco said. “They always see their instructors as their heroes.”
A collection of some of the awards Aakya Manamperi has received for her karate expertise.
Manamperi’s drive to make an impact extends beyond martial arts competition. Outside the dojo, she founded The Girl Shield Project , a student-led organization dedicated to empowering young women through self-defense training, leadership development and health education.
“We do online events, we do in-person events, and so far we’ve reached around 200 different girls in around 20 different countries, and hopefully growing to some more,” Manamperi said.
In addition to her athletic and community achievements, Manamperi maintains a 3.99 GPA at Wayzata High School, where she participates in Science Olympiad and Student Council.
As she prepares to represent the United States in Spain, the weight of her accomplishments is not lost on her.
“Honestly, I appreciate it so much,” Manamperi said. “It’s amazing for me to be able to share things that I like to do and my passions with the world and kind of compete in it. It’s something that I still pinch myself to this day about.”

articles.title_orig: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.title_zh: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.content_orig:
Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been higher still if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

Gypsy Rose Blanchard 's partner Kenan Urker was found dead on his 34th birthday in what officials describe as an apparent drug-related incident, authorities said.
Officers discovered Urker dead when they responded to a call from a home in Raceland, Louisiana, on Thursday evening, according to the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office.
Urker, who was lying on a bed, was cold and his face and arms were blue, according to the sheriff's office. A paper towel on his arm appeared to have "blotches of blood" on it, the sheriff's office said.
On the nightstand next to the bed was a holstered handgun, a syringe and two shot glasses, according to the sheriff's office.
In the bathroom, deputies discovered syringes, a spoon and a "brown powdery substance," the sheriff's office said.
The sheriff's office said there's "no evidence of foul play."
Blanchard wrote on Instagram on Friday, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever."
She added in an Instagram story that he was an "amazing father" and "will forever be my soulmate."
In 2015, Blanchard and her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn were arrested for the fatal stabbing of Blanchard's mother, Clauddinnea "Dee Dee" Blanchard.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was released from prison in 2023 .
"Dee Dee" Blanchard had allegedly abused her daughter for years by convincing Gypsy Rose and the public that she was extremely sick, when she wasn't. "Dee Dee" Blanchard allegedly portrayed her daughter as a frail, disabled child who suffered from multiple illnesses including leukemia and muscular dystrophy, subjecting her to a life in a wheelchair, a feeding tube and unnecessary surgeries.
After her release from prison, Gypsy Rose Blanchard told ABC News she wanted to share her story "to bring awareness to mental health issues, to Munchausen by proxy, to abuse victims."
She said she hoped her story would serve as a "cautionary tale" for others.
