articles.title_orig: Amazon’s $1B plan to combat data center backlash draws more backlash
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s $1B plan to combat data center backlash draws more backlash
articles.content_orig:
On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release , Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.
“For all the claims Amazon makes about investing in carbon-free energy, it conveniently leaves out that it is constructing the single-largest source of climate emissions in the United States in Pecos, Texas,” Stand.Earth said. “Communities will face 33 million tons of harmful air pollution every year—with the power plant using the same amount of energy needed to run more than 1.9 million homes.”
Additionally, Stand.Earth called out Amazon for claiming that most data center generators sparking pollution fears in communities typically sit “idle.” Although Amazon emphasized that most generators only run for “roughly 10 hours per year,” Stand.Earth cited cases where “Amazon data centers ran on diesel back-up power for days at a time.”
At least one part of Amazon’s deal is promising, Stand.Earth suggested. The company ending its practice of using nondisclosure agreements when building new data centers will likely help make projects more transparent.
However, “many of the key concerns communities have are not addressed,” Stand.Earth found. For example, Amazon’s promises to replace all water used for data centers seemingly won’t address “the massive water footprint left by energy infrastructure powering its data centers” or “the potential for forever-chemical contamination from nascent cooling technologies,” Stand.Earth told Ars.
The total amount Amazon is investing also doesn’t seem like much compared to what the company has spent. In the press release, Garman said that Amazon contributed the same amount, more than $1 billion, to data center communities over the past three years.
“Compared to the $220 billion the company is investing in data centers in 2026 alone, Amazon’s commitment of $1 billion over five years for community support is a drop in the bucket,” Stand.Earth said. “It is difficult to read this statement as anything other than a plea from Amazon to continue exploiting communities at minimal cost.”

articles.title_orig: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.title_zh: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.content_orig:
One expert told Marketplace that it could take up to 20 years. People would start tapping into textile waste dumps around the world and, of course, their own closets.
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it ? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here .
Anne Crabbe from Paso Robles, California, asks:
I've always wondered how long it would take for the world to run out of clothes if all production of clothes stopped at once. There are SO many clothes out there (at least here in North America). If the entire world had to use the current supply of all the clothes existing now, when would stores run out? TJ Maxx, Nordstrom Rack, all the thrift stores. I assume (and hope), we would run out of under garments first, then socks, maybe? A ton of assumptions have to be made to answer this, but can it even be answered?
Billions and billions of items of clothing are produced each year, but if clothing production suddenly stopped, snapping up all those garments might take less time than you might think
Depending on your assumptions, it might take up to 20 years for the world to run out of clothing, said Julia DeVoy, who studies the fast-fashion industry and serves as dean of undergraduate programs and students at the Boston College Lynch School of Education and Human Development.
And yes, undergarments and socks would be the first to go, she said.
There would also be a gold rush for materials with higher-quality fiber, like cotton and denim.
"People would want that more, whether it's getting it at a thrift store, or grabbing whatever was on the shelves, or trading with other people who had closets. And there would also be a radical shift towards mending," DeVoy said.
DeVoy estimates that discount and big-box stores in the U.S. would take one month to run out of clothing. These stores operate a just-in time model, which means they only get clothing as needed.
TJX, the parent company of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls, reported its days inventory at 70 days as of mid-2026, which means that shelves would last nine to 10 weeks with zero restocking based on normal demand, DeVoy said. TJX arrives at this figure by taking the existing inventory and dividing it by the current sales rate, DeVoy explained.
But if clothing production stopped, then demand would go up.
"What happened during the pandemic with certain products? People thought they couldn't get hand sanitizer,” DeVoy said. “Basically, what would happen is all the stock on the shelves, because of the just-in-time [model] and the lean inventory that actually sits in the stores, there would be a panic, and all of the existing stock would be wiped out from the store themselves,"
During COVID-19 stockpiling, sales of household staples spiked between 70% to 170% above normal, and spending on stock-up categories ran 70% to 80% above the daily average, DeVoy said.
So if we assume that panic buying doubled demand, which is a conservative estimate, then that would halve the amount of time it would normally take for clothing to run out, leaving discount stores about four to five weeks before clothing ran out, DeVoy said.
People would also look to  thrift stores. Thrift stores are overwhelmed with donations, but they only use about 20% to 30% of the items they receive, DeVoy said. "The remaining 70% to 80% is currently exported, incinerated, or landfilled. This is not because it's all unsellable, but because the humongous volume exceeds available shelf capacity," DeVoy said.
But even if they sold their full backlog instead of incinerating it, DeVoy said they would still sell out in a matter of months.
As stores across the country ran out of clothing, people could tap into other sources that would probably become available. About 100 billion garments are produced a year, with 45 billion garments never reaching the buyer. This is referred to as  "dead stock," which means they're never sold or end up incinerated, DeVoy said.
"There would be this giant hidden reserve that we would keep probably for about the first five years," DeVoy said.
If eight billion people received a modest one to two garments per year, each, that works out to eight to 16 billion garments annually. If there are 45 billion garments, that means there would be three to five years of deadstock, DeVoy said.
There are also massive textile waste dumps around the world, which would now become a vital resource of clothing, and there's a huge surplus of clothing in people's homes, DeVoy said.
The Atacama Desert in Chile receives 131,000 tons of used textiles annually, with over 70%, or 92,000 tons, going directly into landfills or in other illegal dumps, while Ghana's Kantamanto market in Accra receives about 15 million garments a week, of which over 40% becomes direct textile waste, DeVoy said.
"Comparable sites exist all over Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America," DeVoy said.
And people normally only wear 20% of the clothing that they own, with Americans buying 68 new clothing items a year, so they could use the remaining 80% of clothing that's sitting in their closets, DeVoy said.
She estimates that both of these sources of clothing could stretch around 15 years.
One often-cited claim is that we have enough clothing on the planet to last about six generations. But the math and even the original source behind this figure is unclear, according to the BBC, which investigated the claim's origins .
Getting a solid figure is tough – some of those garments in our closet last longer than others, which is just one of the complications that arise when trying to answer this question. "Synthetic fibers tend to last longer and they don't tend to biodegrade very quickly, so we would probably end up with more polyester," said Tasha Lewis, an associate clinical professor in fashion and retail studies at Ohio State University. "We still don't have a good timeline for how long polyester will take to go away because we still have most of it."
We'd also probably think about recycling the clothing that we do have, so we'll still have clothes available to us, Lewis said.
But since clothing production probably won't come to a halt anytime soon, we still have mountains of clothing to deal with. There have been changes in social expectations on how often you should change your clothes and how much variety you should have, said Abigail Clarke-Sather, an associate professor of mechanical and industrial engineering at the University of Minnesota Duluth who's an expert on textile recycling.
"Closet sizes have gotten bigger over the last century because we store so much that we don't know what to do with," Clarke-Sather said.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.title_zh: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight
Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party.
Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!”
In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state . The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol.
“This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing.
Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others.
Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building.
An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens.
Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record.
“This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.”
The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans , all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision.
And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours.
State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments.
“The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson , who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district.
Through continued boos, White said that there was a “ silent majority ” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”.
Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal.
“I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.”
Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”.
“The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.”
Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state.
“If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power.
“We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.”
The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Army creates autonomy command amid Hegseth's robo-warfare push
articles.content_orig:
Installing tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to Pentagon defense board raises conflict-of-interest concerns
Send us your questions about how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midterms
By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, bestowed extraordinary influence on two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting.
The new project, which Hegseth dubbed “Project Meridian” in an event in Quantico, Virginia, on Wednesday, will be led by Pentagon official Emil Michael, a former Uber executive. As the Guardian has reported, Michael made millions in profits off non-public Musk company AI stock while in federal office – and while guiding the Department of Defense’s artificial intelligence efforts.
Along with Luckey and Musk, Project Meridian will also include the Trump loyalist and former speaker of the House Newt Gingrich.
Musk was one of the chief financiers of Trump’s 2024 victory, spending over a quarter of a billion dollars in the run-up to the election. Recent campaign records show he is still a major force in the coming midterms. His America Pac spent $3.4m attacking the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, for example. In the hotly contested Texas Senate race, America Pac spent $6.4m to oppose Democrat James Talarico and $1m to support the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton.
Musk’s SpaceX has been a crucial contractor for US space programs since 2018, and in the second Trump administration his company has emerged as key player in Trump’s pet Golden Dome ballistic missile defense project, a phenomenally expensive effort that could cost as much as $1.2tn.
Musk dwarfs Luckey in resources and fame, but Luckey has achieved immense celebrity in the defense contracting and world. Initially a young celebrity in the tech world for inventing a virtual reality headset, Luckey later founded Anduril, a defense contracting company that has already won significant federal contracts.
Luckey has also become of the most important “bundlers” for Republican candidates on the west coast, as the Guardian reported in August. One of the sources called him the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. Invitations to political fundraisers obtained by the Guardian show Luckey hosted and co-hosted events for candidates from Trump himself to Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, Mehmet Oz, Ted Cruz and others. The most recent event was on 22 August, where he and his wife co-hosted a $50,000-a-head effort to “Keep the Senate”, and listing guests John Thune of South Dakota, Mike Rogers of Michigan, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Jon Husted of Ohio.
It is not necessarily a mystery what Musk and Luckey think about warfare’s future.
The 34-year-old Palmer, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones , UAV s, and space technology , has been already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare. Earlier this year, for example, he said he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict , with vehicles that can “move through he crust of the earth the same way that submarines move through the water”.
He has claimed that his company has “working prototypes of subterranean systems”.
“Bringing major industry players into these types of positions at the Pentagon is not something new, but what feels different now is the substantial financial support these two have, and continue to, deliver for the Republican party,” said Brendan Glavin of Open Secrets, a non-partisan group that tracks campaign spending.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.title_zh: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

This week, Hillsborough County in Florida, which includes Tampa, declared a state of emergency linked to a growing number of dengue cases. So far this year, around 485 cases have been reported in the state , according to the CDC. The disease, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause serious flu-like illness, and one person in Florida has died in the outbreak so far this year, the state’s department of health told media outlets in September.
Seasonal outbreaks of the disease, which affects up to 400 million people worldwide annually , are not unusual in Florida, and they’re often linked to travelers. But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
Dengue, sometimes called dengue fever, is caused by a collection of viruses carried by mosquitoes , primarily Aedes aegypti . Dengue is endemic in a wide swath of the tropics, and usually, most Americans who have the infection acquire it outside of the U.S. during travel. Dengue symptoms can occur 5-7 days after being bitten and range from mild to severe. They may include painful body aches as well as fever and can last up to 10 days .
However, in parts of the U.S. where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes live, they can bite infected people and start to spread the disease locally. “The general pattern that we see—and we've seen this for more than a decade now—is that there are frequent travel-associated cases” in Florida, says Johansson. “We know we have the right vectors there, especially in southern Florida, where there's lots of Aedes aegypti, and there is some local transmission that occurs. Usually that looks like just one or two cases, but sometimes there are small outbreaks.”
In 2009, when two locally acquired infections were identified in Key West, public-health surveillance revealed that a substantial share of people in the town had markers in their blood showing a recent encounter with dengue , even if they hadn’t had symptoms. That suggests that in an outbreak, dengue is likely to be infecting more people than might immediately be clear from case counts.
One distinctive feature of dengue, however, is that the second time someone is infected is likely to be much worse than the first. Sometimes a second infection can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever , which can involve bleeding and a drop in blood pressure, and is sometimes fatal.
This pattern, where the second exposure is more dangerous than the first, has complicated attempts to vaccinate people against the disease. In 2017, Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of the dengue vaccine Dengvaxia, alerted the government of the Philippines that serious dengue infections might occur in people who had received the vaccine as their first exposure to the disease. No dengue vaccine is currently available in the U.S.; Dengvaxia was available starting in 2019 but in 2025 was discontinued by the manufacturer, which cited low demand.
So far, dengue has not established a permanent foothold in the continental U.S., says Johansson. There are a few reasons why that might be: large numbers of people in Florida, where Aedes aegypti thrive, stay within air-conditioned spaces when they’re most active, which means chains of transmission tend to be short.
And the mosquitoes themselves are not particularly adventurous. They tend to stay close to home, within about a 100-meter range, so “it takes people to move the virus around,” says Johansson. If someone who’s infected doesn’t travel, the virus doesn’t either.
There is no cure for dengue; the only treatments are for symptoms. If you are in an area with mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Keep windows closed or use screens, cover as much of your skin as possible with clothing when outdoors, and use mosquito repellent, says Johansson.
Keep yards free of containers that could fill with water and serve as breeding zones for mosquitoes. You’ll have to be vigilant: “These mosquitoes in particular, they can breed in a plastic bag that's collected a little bit of rainwater,” says Johansson.
Cooler weather brings relief. “We're getting to the time of year when things are cooling down, so we should expect a decrease in transmission,” says Johansson. “However, it's still hot in Florida right now”—so it’s not time to drop your guard yet.

articles.title_orig: Kansas enters the chat as Senate map tilts further into red territory
articles.title_zh: Kansas enters the chat as Senate map tilts further into red territory
articles.content_orig:
Senate Leadership Fund is redirecting ad spending from Michael Whatley’s campaign to support other candidates
A major Republican political action committee pulled the plug on financial support for its Senate candidate in North Carolina , Michael Whatley, according to multiple reports, as the party begins to triage resources amid increasingly dire midterm polling.
The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the campaign arm of the Senate majority leader, John Thune, has withdrawn its ad spending in North Carolina to redirect support to other candidates, Semafor reported on Friday. The New York Times, CNN and other publications have confirmed the report with sources close to the fund.
The retirement of Thom Tillis from the US Senate opened the door for Democrats to flip the seat. Former governor Roy Cooper, a venerable presence in the state’s politics, easily won the Democratic nomination. Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, was handpicked by Donald Trump and viewed as a more mainstream candidate than other Republican contenders in the closely contested state.
The SLF had pledged $71m to hold North Carolina’s US Senate seat, and started targeting Cooper before he even won the nomination. The fund ran ads last year trying to link Cooper with the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee, in an unprovoked attack onboard a light-rail train in Charlotte. Cooper was not in office at the time of the attack.
The Pac’s advertising in North Carolina has consistently focused on crime and public safety, featuring a series of interviews with crime victims. Ronald Hayes, whose son Shemar was murdered in 2024, appeared in one such ad. Hayes later said he had been “ swindled ” by the SLF, believing he was going to appear in an advertisement against gun violence and not a political campaign ad.
The SLF had planned to spend $30m more supporting Whatley. But polling data presents an increasingly difficult political map for Republicans trying to hold control of the Senate. Republicans have a 53-47 majority today. With the vice-president, JD Vance, as a tiebreaker, Republicans can afford to lose no more than three seats to keep control.
The Cook Political Report rates the North Carolina Senate race as “leans Democratic”. Seven other races are toss-ups; five are currently held by Republicans, including seats in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Roger Marshall, the senator from Kansas, is facing a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor. Cook rates the race as “leans Republican”.
The SLF reportedly will redirect its North Carolina spending to support Marshall.
Cooper has persistently maintained a polling lead over Whatley despite the deluge of political ads. An AARP poll released on Monday gave Cooper an 11-point lead, consistent with other recent polls. Cooper has never had less than a four-point lead on Whatley in any poll this year.
In-person early voting starts on 15 October in North Carolina.

articles.title_orig: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.title_zh: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.content_orig:
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is in a tight race against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. Will a banking scandal tip the vote?
Sao Paulo, Brazil – It is one of the largest fraud scandals in modern Brazilian history. And experts say it may play a role in the nail-biter race unfolding for Brazil's presidency.
On Sunday, Brazilian voters will head to the polls for the first round of the country's presidential vote.
Centre-left incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80, is currently the frontrunner. He is seeking an unprecedented fourth term, after previously leading the country from 2003 to 2011.
His main challenger is far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, the eldest son of embattled former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for an alleged coup attempt.
The two candidates are locked in a neck-and-neck race. But both have faced fallout from the Banco Master scandal, a sprawling financial scheme that has cast a shadow over Brazil's political sphere.
“I get the sense that the bases of both of these candidacies are not that happy with how the campaigns have gone," said Anthony W Pereira, head of the Stone Center for Latin American Studies at Tulane University.
He pointed to the high levels of rejection Brazilian voters have expressed for both candidates.
In late September, the pollster Quaest found that 56 percent of respondents said they would refuse to vote for Bolsonaro. About 54 percent said the same about Lula.
“Rates of rejection are really high for both candidates. That helps explain why mobilisation and enthusiasm are fairly low,” Pereira said.
One factor in the widespread disillusionment has been the Banco Master scandal. The financial imbroglio has delivered a black eye to both ends of Brazil's political spectrum.
A range of business leaders, political figures, regulators and judges have been swept up in the scandal.
A mid-sized lender, Banco Master grew aggressively over the last decade by selling high-yield deposit certificates. Some of those certificates offered returns of up to 140 percent relative to Brazil’s benchmark interbank rate.
But Banco Master did not have the assets needed to sustain that output.
It lacked the money to pay back its risky loans, and what assets it did have were diverted to shell accounts, according to prosecutors.
Brazil's Central Bank ultimately liquidated Banco Master in 2025, as the lender faced a major funding squeeze.
Its owner, Daniel Vorcaro, was subsequently arrested, accused of an array of financial crimes, including money laundering and fraud.
The collapse of Banco Master triggered a nearly $7.7bn payout from Brazil's Credit Guarantee Fund, the largest disbursement in the nonprofit insurance's history.
Investigators have suggested that Vorcaro protected his fraud scheme by cultivating influence among power brokers among Brazil's elite.
Among those implicated in the scandal is Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate.
Last month, the Supreme Court unsealed documents showing he is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering in connection with Vorcaro.
Audio recordings have also surfaced, appearing to show Bolsonaro soliciting the disgraced bank leader for millions in funding. The money was slated as financing for Dark Horse, a film about his imprisoned father, Jair Bolsonaro.
Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing. He described the interaction as a private sponsorship opportunity, unrelated to the Banco Master scandal.
But while Bolsonaro appears to have direct ties to the scandal, polling suggests that left-wing campaigns like Lula's may suffer more.
In September, the polling institute Datafolha released a survey that found 34 percent of respondents associated the Banco Master scandal more with left-wing politicians than with any other kind of political leaning.
Only 27 percent believed it involved more right-wing politicians.
Another 13 percent associated the scandal with politicians of all stripes, and 16 percent said they did not know how to answer the question.
Leonardo Paz, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV), a think tank, said that Brazilian media shares part of the blame for the public's perception of the scandal.
“Make no mistake, this is a corruption scandal that predominantly involves the right," Paz said.
He argues that the news coverage created a false equivalency between Lula's involvement and Bolsonaro's.
“Flavio’s up to his neck in this scandal, but the press’s need to come across as impartial has ended up generating this inaccurate perception that the Master case affects everyone equally,” Paz explained.
Lula has not been directly linked to the Banco Master scandal.
But revelations have emerged regarding Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, a frequent target of right-wing criticism.
Earlier this year, a rival justice released a document purporting to show Vorcaro composing messages to de Moraes, in some cases asking for legal advice.
De Moraes has denied exchanging any messages with the banker. He has also called the accusations an "incriminating farce for political and electoral purposes".
The justice was appointed to the court in 2017, under then-President Michel Temer, a centre-right figure. But in recent years, de Moraes played an instrumental role in blocking Jair Bolsonaro's attempts to overturn his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election.
De Moraes ultimately oversaw the criminal case that landed the elder Bolsonaro in prison. Bolsonaro's right-wing allies have called that case a political "witch hunt", accusing de Moraes of being beholden to Lula.
"Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes," Flavio Bolsonaro said on the campaign trail this year.
Pereira, the Latin American studies director at Tulane, explained that some members of the public have conflated Lula and de Moraes as a result of the prosecution.
Flavio Bolsonaro has successfully leveraged that perception, Pereira added.
“Flavio is far more implicated [in the Banco Master scandal], but he’s gotten lucky,” he said. “Some lazily assume that Alexandre de Moraes is more or less the same as Lula, so it becomes a wash.”
With Brazil's presidential race expected to be tight, experts warn that even small fluctuations in voter intent could affect the outcome.
Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula is expected to cross the 50-percent threshold needed to avoid a run-off on October 25.
Jorge Chaloub, a political scientist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said the race may ultimately come down to the voters currently backing other candidates.
Also in the running are self-help author Augusto Cury and right-wing figures Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema.
Combined, they are polling at a little more than 10 percent support. Their second-round endorsements could end up deciding the election, according to Chaloub.
“Ideologically, the other candidates are more to the right, and you’d expect them to side with Flavio," Chaloub said.
But, he added, the scandal-plagued race has been volatile so far. Chaloub warned that voters looking for right-wing alternatives may not ultimately side with Bolsonaro, should a run-off occur.
“There’s a reason that those voters didn’t choose Flavio Bolsonaro in the first place," he said.

articles.title_orig: ‘God made Trump’ ad and at least 12 others are part of controversial taxpayer-funded ad campaign
articles.title_zh: ‘God made Trump’ ad and at least 12 others are part of controversial taxpayer-funded ad campaign
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has created at least 13 campaign-style ads as part of its controversial taxpayer-funded, multi-million-dollar effort to promote President Donald Trump and his policies.
Yet-to-be-aired spots include a trio of ads highlighting the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela, one called “God Made Trump” and another recapping the UFC fight he hosted at the White House. Republicans and Democrats alike have questioned the wisdom of spending so much taxpayer money on the ads, which the White House has defended as public service announcements.
CNN has obtained clips of 12 ads, which range from 15 seconds to three minutes long, including two that have already aired. They appear in a Dropbox account — which was shared with CNN — run by LMD, the agency that has been given the government contract for the ad buys. Each ends with “Paid for by the U.S. Government” at the bottom of the screen. Another ad that is not in the Dropbox account, “Final Battle,” has also aired in recent weeks.
The three ads that have already aired have appeared on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. It’s not clear if all of the ads will air on television or digital platforms.
Asked for comment, the White House on Friday afternoon pointed to a just-posted video compilation of the president criticizing CNN.
While each of the ads has a different theme, many of them include imagery of the president and audio with positive reviews from news reports, which is likely to intensify criticism that the campaign is using taxpayer dollars to help Trump personally. They also include patriotic images — including the cap toss at a military graduation, fireworks over Mount Rushmore and military flyovers.
First lady Melania Trump, who has been a rare presence at the White House during the president’s second term, is featured in many of the ads. There are also images from Trump’s reciprocal tariff announcement, the border wall, his escalator presidential-campaign announcement and the tongue-in-cheek framed photograph of an auto pen signifying former President Joe Biden on Trump’s “Presidential Walk of Fame.”
CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.
The ads that have aired so far have spurred widespread condemnation, even as the White House indicates it plans to ramp up its efforts. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.” If Democrats win control of the House next year, he’ll gain congressional subpoena power.
Even some Republicans have criticized the ad campaign.
“Look, if you want to spend money out of your super PAC or other campaign account to communicate that message, that’s fine. It’s not an appropriate PSA. It’s just not, you know, it’s not how we should be spending taxpayer dollars,” said Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina.
Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has said “no” the ads are not an appropriate use of taxpayer dollars. “It’s not even a close question.”
The “UFC 250” ad heavily promotes the company and the June fight that Trump hosted at the White House, prominently featuring UFC CEO Dana White as well as the fighters, the lit-up “claw” over the Octagon and the championship belt.
The “Maduro” spot intersperses a speech by Nicolas Maduro with appearances by Trump and his team at Mar-a-Lago following the Venezuelan dictator’s capture.
And “Military Hype” shows images of fighter jets and unclassified video of what appears to be missile launches. It also includes Trump’s February speech announcing the war with Iran, a conflict which remains deeply unpopular with the American people.
“This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump says in the ad, now seven months into the war.
Some of the ads are starkly political: The two-minute “King of the Jungle” video features images of Trump’s perceived political enemies — former Presidents Barack Obama and Biden, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, all Democrats. There’s video of lions hunting in the wild and a bald eagle sweeping down on the water. A cover of “In the Air Tonight” by In This Moment plays. And Christopher Walken’s lion speech from the 2002 film, “Poolhall Junkies,” is interspersed.
One of the spots, a three-minute-long ad titled “God Made Trump,” was broadcast during Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas. In it, Trump is presented as a messianic figure with a riff on Paul Harvey’s “God Made a Farmer.” It was created by Dilley Meme Team, according to NPR , and began going viral earlier this year.
“I need somebody with arms strong enough to rustle the deep state, and yet gentle enough to deliver his own grandchild. Somebody to ruffle the feathers,” the voiceover says, “So God made Trump.”
The ad “Resilience” shows Trump at multiple points in his life, including early in his New York real estate career, an appearance he made on “The Oprah Winfrey Show,” his descent down the Trump Tower escalator as he announced his candidacy in 2015 and then his time at the White House. In the audio, a reporter refers to him as “the bodyguard of Western Civilization.” His 2023 mugshot from a Fulton County, Georgia, sheriff’s office features prominently, along with video of an assassination attempt on him in Butler, Pennsylvania.
At least an estimated $5.6 million in taxpayer dollars have already been spent on the ads, according to a leading political ad-tracking firm, AdImpact. The actual cost of the taxpayer-funded ad campaign is even higher, but can’t be fully ascertained because public service announcements are subject to different public disclosure rules than campaign ads.
A total of $20 million has been allocated for the effort. The money for these ads is coming from Customs and Border Protection, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Watchdog groups have said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications, but it’s not clear if outside groups have standing to file a lawsuit. Though the ads have received bipartisan criticism, Congress — which groups said had the clearest lane to provide some accountability — has not acted to block the ads.

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.content_orig:
The rapidly expanding capabilities and applications of AI has created a new frontier in higher education. As it is more widely integrated into industry and becoming a highly desired skill, universities are faced with finding effective and ethical ways of teaching the technology and preparing their students for a more technologically savvy workplace.
“Our students are going out into the workplace, and they’re entering a bit of a storm,” said Price Jett, University of Lynchburg’s chief financial officer.
“AI is the highest impacting tool set that we can use to give lifts to businesses. … But it dawned on me that our students are ill prepared, and maybe even some of our professors [are] unaware of what’s going on. … So, we came up with this concept called the [AI] Garage.”
The AI Garage is an agentic AI laboratory where selected students can experiment with building AI agents to solve a company’s real business problems. Jett and Dr. Timothy Schauer, dean of the School of Professional and Applied Sciences, launched the AI Garage as an experiment in the Spring of 2026.
The project brought together businesses, students, and industry experts who Schauer and Jett referred to as “thought accelerators.”
“We talk about ethics — we talk about responsibility — but this isn’t just basic AI where you’re using it to write your papers for you,” said Schauer. “We want it to accomplish things that can be done behind the scenes so that the human doesn’t have to do it, but still stays in the loop.”
Agentic AI goes beyond the generative large language models, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, which typically create content in response to a prompt. Given a goal, an AI agent can determine the necessary steps, use connected tools, and perform tasks independently within defined rules, without requiring a new prompt at every stage. Depending on its purpose and permissions, an agent could analyze data, research information, send emails, schedule meetings, update records, or monitor a process and adjust its actions until the goal is met, all with a “persistent” memory capability similar to a human co-worker.
Of the nearly 30 students who showed interest in joining the pilot cohort, only seven were selected. Working in teams, the students spent four weeks at the end of the spring semester creating solutions to the real-world problems provided to them by four business executives.
The AI Garage was set up in Schewel Hall on special computers that were not connected to the University’s network. Schauer and Jett worked closely with Lynchburg’s IT department when setting up the lab to create a “walled garden” where the students would be able to safely work with their AI agents.
The students selected for the Garage had to be dedicated to the work, willing to put in the necessary time and effort even while finishing their course work and preparing for final exams and projects.
“These students were in this room — they ate there, some of them slept there,” said Schauer. “We’d come in in the morning, sometimes they worked all night. They were there on the weekends. They were very motivated.”
One of these students was Kristofer Hickson ʼ26, a veteran who transferred to Lynchburg after completing his associate degree at Central Virginia Community College.
“I’m not a computer science person,” said Hickson, a business major. “I have trouble finding my way around my own email. … [but] I can stumble my way around things and find my way into it.”
Hickson began experimenting with generative AI as he searched for work, using large language models, or LLMs, to refine and improve his resumes and cover letters so they better aligned with a given job description. Over time he became exhausted with manually prompting the LLM to do this work so he asked it to create a program that would do it automatically and upload and export to a file on his computer.
A few months before the AI Garage was launched, Hickson explained what he had been doing to Dr. Eric Kyper, a professor of business and economics. Kyper recognized that Hickson had stumbled into agentic AI and through their conversation, Hickson began thinking about what pursuing agentic AI could mean for his future.
Khurshid Kazimi ʼ28, an accounting major, was another student in the first AI Garage cohort. When she learned about the project, she immediately jumped at the opportunity.
“The first two weeks of working on building the AI agent was so difficult,” said Kazimi, an international student from Afghanistan. “And one thing that I realized later was that Price Jett and Dr. Schauer — they were not sharing all the information with us. … We were completely lost.”
Kazimi explained that Schauer and Jett wanted the students to take initiative and have the curiosity to figure out the next steps on their own. She was appreciative of the approach they took, saying, “They did the absolute best thing.”
She was also appreciative of her fellow students and the various talents each brought to the AI Garage.
“When we’re working together, we can find out the things that we cannot find out when we’re working alone,” Kazimi said.
“We were working on the same thing [and] I was not realizing a problem,” she explained. “I didn’t have that mindset to look at the problem in the same way … and then my teammate — she was finding out the thing that I couldn’t.”
At the end of the four-week period, the students presented their work to executives from each company. All of the companies involved wanted to use the tools the students created for them.
“The goal was not to give something valuable to a company, although that happened,” said Jett. “The goal [was] to teach our students how to solve business problems and give lift to businesses. That’s what businesses expect from us at the University.
“I think that’s our responsibility as leaders at the University to do that.”
Schauer added, “I do think that those universities that teach [AI] responsibly will put their students in a better position to actually get jobs and create value for companies. You can’t ignore that.”
Three students, including Hickson and Kazimi, were immediately offered internships or full-time employment.
“[Companies] don’t want people with computer science degrees,” said Hickson. “They want people with accounting skills, business skills, marketing skills, who know how to use agentic AI.”
He added, “I got a lot of confidence because [of] everything I built from scratch in the [AI] Garage. … It got me where I’m at and has helped give me the confidence to tread a little further.”
Schauer and Jett are now running the second round of the AI Garage this semester with four new businesses. For more information about the AI Garage, contact Schauer at [email protected] .

Falcon Heavy launched its first NRO mission while SpaceX landed four boosters in one day.
SpaceX closed out one of its busiest days ever with a midnight Falcon Heavy launch from Florida, and the rocket’s two side boosters came home to finish off a landing record the company had never set before.
Falcon Heavy lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:54 p.m. ET Thursday carrying NROL-97, a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office. It was the first time the NRO has flown on Falcon Heavy after 22 missions on Falcon 9, and the first NRO mission bought through the National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 2 contract awarded in 2025, according to Spaceflight Now .
Falcon Heavy lifts off from pad 39A in Florida for the 14th time! pic.twitter.com/uuZLKNTdD7
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
Roughly eight minutes after liftoff, side boosters B1104 and B1072 touched down at Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, setting off double sonic booms across Brevard County. B1104 was flying for the second time and B1072 for the fourth. Both last flew on August 30 on NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, making NROL-97 the quickest turnaround between Falcon Heavy missions to date. The brand new center core, B1106, was expended in the Atlantic so the payload could reach its high energy orbit, and SpaceX’s mission page noted the fairing had previously flown on the NROL-95 mission in July.
The two landings capped a record for SpaceX. Earlier Thursday, Falcon 9 booster B1101 returned to Landing Zone 40 after sending the Crew-13 astronauts to the International Space Station , and another Falcon 9 launched the Transporter-18 rideshare with 130 payloads from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Spaceflight Now reported it was the first time SpaceX has landed four boosters in a single day, wrapping up the triple header Teslarati previewed on Wednesday .
Falcon Heavy’s side boosters land on LZ-1 and LZ-2 pic.twitter.com/dBPcNeggFx
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
The mission also brought Landing Zone 1 back for what may be its final landing. SpaceX first landed an orbital class booster there in December 2015, but its lease on the former Launch Complex 13 site ended in 2025 as the company moved Florida landings to new pads at its own launch complexes. With LZ-40 already holding the Crew-13 booster, SpaceX brought LZ-1 back into service for one more night. Launch tracker Next Spaceflight listed NROL-97 as the final expected landing at the site.
NROL-97 adds to a fast growing stack of national security work for SpaceX. The company has flown four Space Force missions from Vandenberg since mid August, several believed to carry Starshield satellites, pushing its Pentagon contract total for 2026 past $8 billion . Elon Musk was also named this week to help lead the Pentagon’s Project Meridian study on the future of warfare.
The Florida doubleheader stood out for another reason. The Space Coast saw only one launch in all of September as SpaceX shifts more of its East Coast infrastructure toward Starship, which reached orbit for the first time on Flight 14 just three days earlier.

Tesla Full Self-Driving is set to receive improvements to address its two biggest issues, according to a company engineer.
Director of Engineering at Tesla AI, Phil Duan, revealed in a post on X that improvements to both pothole avoidance and navigation “are coming,’ something we have heard many times in the past. However, there are a few things that seem to hint that things might be different this time around.
Improvements on both are coming.
— Phil Duan (@pduan) October 1, 2026
Pothole avoidance, navigation, speed control, and left lane camping are some of the most prevalent and frequently mentioned shortcomings of the Full Self-Driving suite. These are a few of the biggest issues that have kept Tesla Full Self-Driving as a Supervised suite, meaning drivers must remain attentive during operation .
Pothole avoidance was first mentioned as an “Upcoming Improvement” with the Tesla Full Self-Driving v14.3 update back in early April of this year. It was listed alongside “Expand reasoning to all behaviors beyond destination handling.”
Tesla is fixing Full Self-Driving’s pothole problem
It’s been six months since we first saw pothole avoidance explicitly mentioned , and it has not moved beyond that and joined the main release notes yet.
Tesla has not shed any light on why pothole avoidance has been such an issue for it to solve, but it also has issues identifying large bumps much of the time, so its modeling of sudden changes in road conditions is likely pretty weak at this particular point. I’ve had more issues with large bumps than potholes, personally, but both are issues that need to be resolved.
This is that big bounce that I mentioned in the quoted post.
It’s just a tad too drastic to take at the speed FSD wants to go over it. You can see me quickly swipe down into Sloth, but I intervened. https://t.co/K20PK9ysBg pic.twitter.com/81Oc82ZJcZ
— TESLARATI (@Teslarati) August 2, 2026
It makes sense that things might be pretty close to being released to the public, as we are going on such an extensive period of time between it being mentioned and it actually being deployed.
Navigation is likely the most painful part of using Full Self-Driving , as it routinely takes strange routes, has trouble with local rules (like Except Right Turn Stop Signs in Pennsylvania), and sometimes does not realize that maneuvers it is suggesting are against the law. Turning out of my neighborhood, you cannot turn left, yet my Model Y still suggests it roughly 70 percent of the time when I’m leaving.
However, Tesla might be close to a breakthrough on this . With the Summer Update, Tesla added “Preferred Routes” alongside “Automatic Navigation.”
Preferred Routes prioritized roads that the driver had actually taken before, instead of always defaulting to what the vehicle believes is the most efficient path. This has already solved many of my issues. Formerly, I would turn off the Online Routing setting, and that would eliminate most of my complaints with routing, but then you lose out later on the Live Traffic Visualization.
Tesla’s Navigation has improved tremendously thanks to the Preferred Routes release with the Summer Update, but it still could use some polishing , as it still suggests strange routes from time to time, and it also has a lot of issues getting out of a parking lot. I find that those truly confuse FSD sometimes.

articles.title_orig: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
The Goddard School of Littleton celebrated World News Day by transforming students into “junior journalists” for a day on Sept. 28
For one day, students at The Goddard School of Littleton became junior journalists.
Wearing ties and carrying cardboard microphones, children interviewed classmates as part of the school’s first World News Day celebration. The activity was designed to encourage curiosity and help students practice asking questions.
“World News Day really ties into our curriculum that focuses on teaching the students how we ask questions,” said Erin Davis, co-owner of The Goddard School of Littleton. “It asks how we can dive a bit deeper and be investigative.”
The Goddard School of Littleton is a private early childhood education program serving infants, toddlers, preschoolers and pre-kindergarten students. Nearly 700 Goddard Schools locations across the country participated in World News Day this year, according to Chas Kurtz, the organization’s senior public relations manager.
“The idea came from a natural connection we saw between young children and journalists: both are constantly asking questions to better understand the world around them,” Kurtz said.
Becoming a “junior journalist” embodies The Goddard School’s Wonder of Learning program, which is an inquiry-based program that employs a STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math) approach to its curriculum.
“(World News Day) also gave us an opportunity to bring Wonder of Learning to life because inquiry-based learning isn’t simply about arriving at the ‘right’ answer; it's about helping children learn how to think, explore and continue asking questions,” Kurtz said.
In The Goddard School of Littleton’s gym, kids lined up outside the hallway and were granted permission to enter by their teacher one by one. They sat and waited for instruction from their team of teachers — usually a pair or group comprised of a lead and assistant teacher.
On the walls were different stations for the students to explore. One station was a press conference set up with a table and props.
Students took turns sitting at the table and answering questions from their peers, like “How is your day?” and “What are you going to be for Halloween?”
Davis, who runs and owns the Littleton school with her husband, Andrew, said each class had its own lesson plan revolved around journalism.
“Our toddlers had newspaper prints to get that exposure to real-world materials,” Davis said.
Jess Reynolds, one of the directors at the Goddard School of Littleton, helped arrange the gym for World News Day to go beyond lesson planning, Davis said.
“It works because it’s a combination of taking what maybe couldn’t fully come to fruition in a classroom and building a better space for that,” she said of the gym activities.
Two children and Jess Reynolds, a director at the Goddard School of Littleton, sit at the press conference table in the gym on Sept. 28
As the kids rotated between being the interviewer and the interviewee, Reynolds and Davis hopped around different classrooms to help and see what the students were up to. Reynolds, who also works on social media promotion for the school, took videos of two students talking about their weekends and asking each other questions.
“It’s awesome to see what they come up with and see them think through their questions and answers,” she said.
In the class with 2-year-olds, they colored in comics and food illustrations for a food review column.
Other classes had a map of the state with clouds, a sun, and raindrops to experience meteorology reporting.
Asking questions gives children power, Kurtz said.
“Asking ‘why,’ ‘how’ or ‘what if’ is one of the ways children learn to make sense of the world. And when they ask a question, listen to someone else’s perspective, investigate an idea and share what they discover, they’re building skills that extend far beyond journalism,” he said. “They’re learning to think critically, communicate, problem-solve and remain curious.”
According to Davis, helping students grasp the basics of various media forms, ranging from news articles to television programming, is important.
That fundamental principle inspired the creation of World News Day: the belief that journalists bear the responsibility of delivering trustworthy news and information essential to supporting both citizens and a democratic society.
World News Day is celebrated annually on Sept. 28, and The Goddard School may continue its junior journalist trend next year.
“We’ve especially loved seeing the celebration extend beyond the classroom by connecting local media with our students and staff and bringing our wider communities together to celebrate journalism,” Kurtz said. “We’re looking forward to learning from this year’s experience and exploring how we can build on our World News Day celebration in the future.”
Davis said after World News Day wraps up for The Goddard School of Littleton, she would be interested in celebrating again next year.
“One of the great things about our curriculum and our teachers is that we can try new things and grow them every time and focus on adaptability,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.title_zh: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.content_orig:
Real-world data show Lybalvi cuts acute care visits in schizophrenia or bipolar I with AUD, while long-acting aripiprazole offers flexible dosing and stable symptom control.
Retrospective claims analysis data showed significant reductions in hospital and emergency department visits after initiation of Lybalvi (olanzapine/samidorphan) among patients with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder and comorbid alcohol use disorder (AUD), according to Hemangi Panchmatia, MS. Acute care events were measured in 4 categories: all-cause, mental health–related, disease-related, and AUD-related. "We saw a significant reduction across all of these 4 categories in our schizophrenia patients as well as bipolar I disorder patients who have a comorbid alcohol use disorder," Panchmatia said.
Samidorphan, an opioid antagonist with strong binding at the mu receptor, was combined with olanzapine to attenuate weight gain and metabolic dysfunction. Peripheral effects included glucose metabolism and fat accumulation, whereas central effects on the brain's reward system may have supported satiety and reduced cravings.  Antecedent studies fed into a long-term open-label extension lasting up to 4 years or beyond for many patients, and mitigation of weight gain and metabolic dysfunction was associated with better adherence and longer persistence. 1 Many patients had no significant weight gain, and metabolic parameters remained stable over a long period. Findings extended across schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder and across patients early in illness and those more typical of clinical trials. "It's important to provide your patients with an efficacious treatment that they can adhere to, that they can tolerate, and that they will stay on for long periods of time," McGrory said.
A separate clinician-focused poster summarized the development program for aripiprazole lauroxil, a long-acting injectable prodrug formulated to reduce absorption. This design allowed extended release with consistent, predictable plasma concentrations and without pronounced peak and trough effects, maintaining patients at levels relevant to their symptoms. Dosing once monthly, every 6 weeks, or every 2 months allowed clinicians to individualize intervals. Significant symptom reductions were observed on the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale, with improvement on the Clinical Global Impression–Severity scale. 2 The adverse event profile mirrored that of oral aripiprazole over an extended period, including low sedation and lower levels of metabolic dysfunction and weight gain.
Dr McGrory is medical strategy lead for psychiatry and senior medical director & product lead at Alkermes.
Ms Panchmatia is senior director and head of psychiatry HEOR at Alkermes.
1. Jain R, Penn A, Carbray J, et al. Acute care events following initiation of olanzapine/samidorphan among patients with schizophrenia or bipolar 1 disorder and comorbid alcohol use disorder. Poster presented at: Psych Congress 2026 Annual Meeting; September 15-19; New Orleans, LA. Accessed September 18, 2026.
2. Kempf B, Carbray J, Barbee R, et al. Use of an aripiprazole lauroxil injection administered once every month, 6 weeks, or 2 months in people with schizophrenia: a clinician focused summary of study data. Poster presented at: Psych Congress 2026 Annual Meeting; September 15-19; New Orleans, LA. Accessed September 18, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Cornell rape case: Letitia James named special prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Cornell rape case: Letitia James named special prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- The Cornell rape accuser was "failed" by people obligated to protect her, including police and the prosecutor, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said at a news conference on Friday.
A visibly outraged Hochul blasted Cornell University Police, the Tompkins County district attorney and the state's rape laws before introducing Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the controversial case
James told a packed news conference at the governor's office that this is now "an active criminal investigation." She pledged a full and fair investigation.
"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard, that is the promise of our justice system," James said.
Hochul said the system failed Jane Doe. Information from her interview with police was not passed to the district attorney, who then failed to interview her.
"I am deeply disturbed by Cornell University's police and how they handled this," Hochul said. She said sending a "partial record" to the district attorney was a failure.
"In what world would the police learn from the victim that she had literally been gang raped" and that she believed "100%" she had been raped and not elevate those allegations, Hochul said.
Hochul claimed the Tompkins County district attorney then did not do the "bare minimum" and interview the woman after receiving the six-page police report.
"In what world does the district attorney not interview her or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked again. That is "exactly why we're here today and why I took the action last night ."
Tompkins County District Attorney Matt Van Houten told ABC News that CUPD's six-page summary of Jane Doe's allegations convinced him no crime occurred.
Hochul also took the opportunity to call for a change in the state law around voluntary intoxication in cases of sexual assault. She said lawmakers must address this part of the law as soon as possible.
Jane Doe's attorney said he and his client are "pleased" the governor appointed a special prosecutor because "contradictions between the district attorney's statements and those of the Cornell police have been shocking."
Van Houten said Friday he supports the governor's decision to remove him from the case and pledged his cooperation with the attorney general.
Cornell has also endorsed Hochul's decision to remove the DA from the case and assign it to James.
"We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State's rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case," a spokesperson said.

articles.title_orig: When should I get the flu shot? What experts say is the ideal time to protect yourself
articles.title_zh: When should I get the flu shot? What experts say is the ideal time to protect yourself
articles.content_orig:
Should you get your flu shot with a Covid vaccine? Here’s the guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
It’s October and time for flu shots.
Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV.
Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands.
Vaccination isn’t “a guarantee that we’re going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk” of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians.
Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn't updated its advice.
Now doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them.
Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids.
The vaccines don't block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults' hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota.
Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal.
The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna's mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot.
The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they're ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria.
COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk.
Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it.
With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson.
Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi.
Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.
Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots.
While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they're most common in pharmacies.
For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. For example, Walgreens says it offers those shots without a prescription in all but two states, Arizona and Oregon, but can provide doses for children as young as 3 in some states while others have higher age limits.
Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it.
Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it's also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn’t want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together.
RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults.
The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems.
It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren't vaccinated and some other high-risk babies.
